opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the brain is really the existence proof. It's the thing that tells you this is possible at all. You've got roughly twenty watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, and it's doing perception, motor control, planning, language, all in this incredibly noisy, warm, wet environment. If you look at it from the perspective of a traditional digital computing engineer, it's a nightmare. The components are unreliable, the signals are stochastic, neurotransmitter release at a synapse is probabilistic, ion channels open and close randomly due to thermal fluctuations. And yet it works, and it works remarkably efficiently.

The way I see it, the brain isn't fighting the noise, it's using it. In digital computing, we spend an enormous amount of energy suppressing thermal fluctuations. We push transistors to operate at voltages far above the thermal noise floor so that a zero is reliably a zero and a one is reliably a one. Then, ironically, when we want to do probabilistic machine learning, sampling, generative modeling, Bayesian inference, we go and simulate randomness in software with pseudo-random number generators. So we pay energy to kill the noise, and then pay energy again to fake it. That's a huge inefficiency.

The brain seems to skip that step. A lot of computational neuroscience points toward the brain doing something like probabilistic inference, sampling from distributions over hypotheses about the world, and the stochasticity of neurons is a natural substrate for that. The physics of the system is doing part of the computation. That's essentially what thermodynamic computing is about: building hardware where the natural dynamics of a physical system, fluctuations, dissipation, relaxation toward equilibrium or through non-equilibrium steady states, map directly onto the algorithm you want to run, like sampling from an energy-based model or diffusion-style generative processes.

I'd add a caveat, though. I don't think we need to copy the brain. Neuromorphic computing has tried to mimic spikes and neurons pretty literally, with mixed results. The lesson I take is more about principles than biology: computation is physical, intelligence is fundamentally probabilistic, and if you embrace the thermodynamics instead of fighting it, you can get orders of magnitude better energy efficiency. The brain shows the ceiling is way higher than where our current GPUs sit, and that gap is the opportunity.

r001.rationale: The response calls the brain an “existence proof” and describes its broad capabilities and efficient computation, communicating it as proof that a highly capable computer is possible.

r002.rationale: It mentions probabilistic neurotransmitter release and stochastic neural activity, but does not identify neurotransmitter reaction networks described by master equations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I like to think about it is that the brain is a proof of existence. It's a physical system that runs on about 20 watts, roughly a lightbulb, and it's doing inference, learning, planning, all of this in a wet, warm, noisy environment. Every neuron is sitting in a bath of thermal fluctuations. Ion channels open and close stochastically. Synaptic vesicle release is probabilistic. If you were an engineer coming from the digital world, you'd look at that and say this is a terrible substrate, there's noise everywhere, how could it possibly compute? And yet it works, and it works at an energy efficiency that is many orders of magnitude beyond what we do with GPUs.

So the question is, how? And I think the answer is that the brain isn't fighting the noise, it's using it. Digital computing is built on this premise that you want to suppress fluctuations. You spend a huge amount of energy pinning bits to zero or one, well away from the thermal floor, so that nature can't flip them on you. That costs you. Landauer tells you there's a floor, but in practice we're something like a million times above it because we're constantly paying to keep entropy out.

The brain does something different. A lot of what intelligence actually is, in the Bayesian sense, is sampling. You have a posterior over what's going on in the world, you need to draw samples from it, you need to explore hypotheses, you need to make decisions under uncertainty. And sampling from a probability distribution is exactly what a thermodynamic system does for free. A physical system coupled to a heat bath relaxes toward a Boltzmann distribution. The noise is the randomness source. So if you can shape the energy landscape of your physical system so that its equilibrium distribution is the distribution you care about, then the physics does the inference for you, and the thermal fluctuations that a digital engineer would call errors are actually the thing doing the work.

There's a lot of evidence that this is what's happening in cortex. Neural variability looks like sampling. You see trial to trial fluctuations in responses that are well described by the brain drawing samples from a posterior rather than computing a point estimate. Spontaneous activity in visual cortex, when there's no input, looks like the prior, and it gets shaped by learning to match the statistics of the inputs. That's exactly what you'd expect from a system that's doing probabilistic inference by stochastic dynamics. Dendritic processing is analog. Synaptic plasticity rules look like they're doing something like gradient descent on a free energy, which is a thermodynamic quantity. The whole predictive processing, free energy principle framework that Friston and others pushed is basically saying the brain is a non-equilibrium thermodynamic system that minimizes surprise, and the math is the same math as statistical physics.

And this was really the insight behind what we were doing at Extropic. We looked at the history of computing and said, we went through a phase where everything was digital and deterministic because that's what the transistor was good at and because we were climbing Moore's law. But the workloads have changed. Generative AI is fundamentally about sampling from complicated distributions. We're doing that today by taking a deterministic machine and bolting on pseudo-random number generators and burning enormous amounts of energy to simulate randomness on hardware that was built to eliminate it. That's a mismatch between the computational primitive and the physical substrate. The brain shows you that the other approach is viable. Nature already found it. Evolution ran a billion year optimization on energy efficient inference and it landed on a noisy, analog, thermodynamic machine, not a clean digital one.

So when people ask me is the brain thermodynamic computing, I'd say it's the strongest piece of empirical evidence we have that an intelligence can be built on physics that embraces fluctuations instead of suppressing them. It's not that we want to copy neurons. I'm not that interested in biological fidelity. It's that the brain tells you the design space is real. There exists a region of the design space where you get general intelligence at 20 watts by letting the thermodynamics do the computing, and the question for us as engineers is how do we get there with a substrate we can actually fabricate and scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the brain is an existence proof that you can do remarkably sophisticated computation with a relatively small energy budget, using components that are noisy and imperfect. That should make us question how much of our current computing architecture is necessary for intelligence, and how much is a consequence of the particular engineering path we took.

In a conventional computer, we spend energy making the physical substrate behave like a reliable, deterministic abstraction. We suppress fluctuations so that a bit does what we expect. The thermodynamic computing perspective asks: could we design systems where some of those fluctuations actually help perform the computation? For example, noise can help a system explore possibilities rather than getting trapped in one configuration.

The brain is suggestive because its computation is inseparable from its physical dynamics. Neurons and synapses are dissipative, fluctuating systems, continually consuming energy. But I’d distinguish that observation from the stronger claim that the brain implements a particular thermodynamic computing algorithm. The brain doesn’t establish that for us.

What it gives us is a reason to investigate the approach: intelligence can emerge in a physical system that operates with noise, under tight energy constraints. Perhaps we can build machines whose physics does more of the computational work directly, instead of having to simulate all of that physics on a digital machine.

r001.rationale: The response calls the brain an existence proof of remarkably sophisticated computation and links that capability to intelligence, presenting it as evidence that a physical system can compute effectively.

r002.rationale: The response discusses noisy, dissipative neural dynamics but does not mention neurotransmitter reaction networks or their description by master equations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the brain is an existence proof that you can do remarkably sophisticated computation with noisy, energy-constrained physical hardware. But we should be careful: that doesn’t establish that the brain implements any particular thermodynamic computing architecture.

The interesting thing is that the brain doesn’t first eliminate all the noise and then compute on perfectly reliable bits. It operates with fluctuations, and it’s continually exchanging energy and matter with its environment. So the question is: can we build machines where that physical dynamics actually helps perform the computation, rather than being something we spend energy suppressing?

For example, if your task involves sampling from a probability distribution, fluctuations can be a resource. You can try to engineer a system whose natural evolution produces the samples you want. Then the physics is doing useful computational work.

So I see the brain as motivation for exploring that design space. It shows us that intelligence is compatible with noisy, dissipative hardware. Understanding exactly which physical mechanisms make it efficient—and which of those we can reproduce in engineered systems—is the harder question.
